c.tagline: A sprawling Red Sea resort city with reef-fringed islands, diving, and Egypt's largest aquarium
langs: German and Russian (common due to tourism)

card: Widely accepted at hotels and larger restaurants; cash useful for El Dahar market and taxis

taxi.fare: Negotiated flat rate, as meters are uncommon
taxi.fareNote: Agree the fare before departure; hotel-arranged transfers are common

emergency.note: Tourist police (180) can assist with English-language support

english.label: Easy to get by in English

walk: Sekalla and El Mamsha waterfront strips are walkable; El Dahar and other districts require a taxi given the city's sprawl

safety.safety: Generally safe in the resort and tourist zones, with a visible tourist police presence
safety.crime: Petty theft and persistent vendors/touts in markets are the main practical concerns

hood_landmark.El Dahar: El Dahar's traditional souks and Al Mina Mosque
hood_landmark.Sekalla (El Saqqala): Sekalla's busy Sheraton Road hotel and shopping strip
hood_landmark.El Ahyaa: El Ahyaa's residential and mid-range resort area

avoid.reason: Expect aggressive touts, taxi overcharging, and dive/excursion booking scams in Sheraton Road and El Dahar bazaar areas — agree prices in advance.

hood_desc: The oldest part of Hurghada, with traditional bazaars, cheaper eats, and the long-distance bus station.
The historic tourist core along Sheraton Road, packed with hotels, shops, and restaurants.

A pedestrianised seafront promenade of restaurants, cafes, bars and shops running south of Sekalla through the New Town, on the road out towards Hadaba and Sahl Hasheesh. The beach hotels lined up behind it make it the easiest base for eating and drinking on foot in the evening.
A quieter, more residential district with mid-range and budget resorts, less central than Sekalla.

A purpose-built resort bay about 25 km south of central Hurghada, laid out around a long crescent beach and the Old Town Piazza of restaurants, shops and an arrival plaza. Nearly every property here is a large five-star all-inclusive with its own house reef, so it suits diving and beach holidays rather than city life.
lodging: The Oberoi Beach Resort Sahl Hasheesh

water.note: Drink bottled water only; avoid ice of unknown origin outside resorts.

transit.sys: Local minibuses along the main coastal road; hotel shuttles common
transit.hours: Minibuses run roughly daylight to evening hours
transit.map: Not centrally published; ask locally for minibus routes
transit.note: Most visitors rely on taxis or hotel-arranged transport given the city's spread-out layout

transport.air: Hurghada International Airport (HRG), about 15-20 min from Sekalla
transport.train: No passenger rail service to Hurghada
transport.bus: Long-distance buses connect to Cairo, Luxor, and other Egyptian cities
transport.ferry: Seasonal boats connect to Sharm El Sheikh across the Red Sea
transport.car: Rental cars available; most visitors use taxis and hotel transfers

net.w: Free wifi standard in hotels and cafes
net.ops: Vodafone Egypt, Orange Egypt, Etisalat Misr
net.fwn: Free wifi widely available in hotels
net.ap: A Vodafone or Orange Egypt tourist SIM or eSIM

tip.s: 10-15% is customary for dive guides and tour operators
tip.r: 10% is standard, though often added automatically at resort restaurants

food.name: Sayadeya
food.desc: Red Sea fish baked over rice cooked in spiced tomato and caramelised onion stock; the coast's signature one-pot dinner.

places.name: El Halaka Fish Restaurant
places.note: Pick your fish off the ice; simple, fresh and mid-priced with harbour tables.

places.name: Star Fish Restaurant
places.note: Long-running marina fish house where you choose the catch and the cooking method.

food.name: Grilled Red Sea fish and seafood tagen
food.desc: Whole fish, calamari and prawns grilled over charcoal or baked in a clay tagen with tomato, garlic and cumin, sold by weight.

places.name: El Dahar fish restaurants
places.note: The cheapest genuinely local seafood in Hurghada, well away from the resort strip.

places.name: El Halaka Fish Restaurant
places.note: Charcoal-grilled catch of the day with salads and baladi bread.

food.name: Koshari
food.desc: Egypt's carb-stacked national street dish: rice, lentils and macaroni under spiced tomato sauce, chickpeas, crisp onions and garlic vinegar.

places.name: Abou Tarek
places.note: Koshari specialist; one bowl feeds most people for the price of a coffee.

places.name: GAD Restaurant
places.note: Reliable 24-hour Egyptian chain; koshari, grills and shawarma at local prices.

food.name: Feteer meshaltet
food.desc: Flaky layered pastry brushed with ghee and baked until crisp, served plain with honey and cheese or stuffed savoury like a pie.

places.name: Nimlayah
places.note: Popular for feteer and Egyptian sweets; watch the dough spun at the counter.

places.name: El Dahar bakeries
places.note: Old-town ovens sell feteer by weight, sweet or savoury, from early morning.

food.name: Molokhia
food.desc: Finely chopped jute leaves cooked into a glossy green soup with garlic and coriander, poured over rice with chicken or rabbit.

places.name: GAD Restaurant
places.note: Dependable molokhia with rice and grilled chicken, open around the clock.

places.name: El Dahar local kitchens
places.note: Small family restaurants around the souq do the home-style version best.

food.name: Foul and taameya breakfast
food.desc: Slow-stewed fava beans with cumin, lemon and oil beside taameya, Egypt's herb-flecked fava falafel, scooped up with hot baladi bread.

places.name: El Dahar street stalls
places.note: Carts start before dawn; a full breakfast costs almost nothing.

places.name: GAD Restaurant
places.note: Sit-down version with fresh bread and salads if the carts feel intimidating.

food.name: Karkade
food.desc: Deep-red hibiscus tea drunk iced in the heat or hot after dinner, tart and lightly floral; Egypt's most recognisable soft drink.

places.name: El Dahar souq cafes
places.note: Traditional ahwas serve karkade with shisha and backgammon under the awnings.

places.name: Marina Boulevard cafes
places.note: Iced karkade with a harbour view; pricier but pleasant at sunset.

food.name: Asab (sugarcane juice)
food.desc: Cane pressed to order through a clattering roller mill into a glass of cloudy, grassy-sweet juice; drink it fresh, within minutes.

places.name: El Dahar juice stalls
places.note: Green-tiled juice shops along the main street press cane all day for pennies.

places.name: Sekalla juice bars
places.note: Also good for mango, guava and lemon-mint if cane is too sweet.

landmarks: Giftun Islands
Hurghada's postcard paradise of blinding-white sandbars and coral gardens, where day boats anchor for snorkeling in impossibly turquoise Red Sea shallows.
El Mina Mosque (Al Mina Grand Mosque)
The city's grandest landmark, a twin-minareted waterfront mosque whose cream domes glow at sunset over the fishing harbour.
Hurghada Marina
A pastel-painted yacht harbour of promenades, cafés and boutiques, the city's favorite evening strolling ground with mosque views across the water.
El Dahar Old Town and Bazaar
Hurghada's original quarter, where haggling for spices, shisha pipes and souvenirs in the souk delivers an authentic slice of everyday Egypt.
Hurghada Museum
A polished antiquities museum spanning pharaonic treasures to Islamic art, bringing 4,000 years of Egyptian civilization to the Red Sea coast.
Sand City Hurghada
An open-air museum of monumental sand sculptures, from sphinxes to movie characters, improbably carved and preserved in the desert sunshine.
Hurghada Grand Aquarium
A family-friendly complex with a walk-through underwater tunnel showcasing Red Sea sharks, rays and reef life alongside a mini zoo and rainforest zone.
Orange Bay Island
A dazzling beach islet off Giftun with swing seats in gin-clear water, the Red Sea's most Instagrammed swimming stop.
Dolphin House Reef (Sha'ab El Erg)
A horseshoe reef north of Hurghada where snorkelers regularly swim alongside resident pods of playful spinner dolphins.
Eastern Desert Bedouin villages and dunes
Quad-bike and jeep safaris race into the Red Sea mountains for Bedouin tea, camel rides and blazing desert sunsets behind Hurghada.

train.note: There is no railway to Hurghada - Egyptian National Railways runs along the Nile valley and the Delta, not down the Red Sea coast. The nearest station is at Qena, about 3-4 hours inland by road, with trains to Luxor and Cairo. Most visitors fly into Hurghada International Airport or take the coach.

bus.note: No international coaches. Go Bus (https://go-bus.com/) and Blue Bus run frequently from the Hurghada terminal to Cairo in about 6 hours, Luxor in 4-5 and Sharm El Sheikh via Suez; book online, as the good services sell out. Superjet also covers the Cairo route.

intl.to: Sharm El Sheikh (Egypt) - across the Gulf of Suez, service intermittent
intl.op: Red Sea fast-ferry operators — check current status locally

ferry.note: There are no international sailings from Hurghada, and the cross-gulf catamaran to Sharm El Sheikh has been suspended and revived repeatedly over the years - verify before counting on it, as the road route via Suez takes eight hours or more. Boats from the marina are dive and snorkelling excursions to Giftun Island and the reefs.

full.name: Luxor
full.blurb: The Valley of the Kings and Karnak Temple complex, reached by a roughly three-hour drive across the Eastern Desert from Hurghada.

full.name: Cairo & Giza Pyramids
full.blurb: The Great Pyramids of Giza and the Grand Egyptian Museum, reachable by a short domestic flight or a long overland drive from Hurghada.

full.name: Wadi El Gemal National Park (Marsa Alam)
full.blurb: A protected coastal reserve south of Marsa Alam with mangroves, coral reefs, and Bedouin communities, roughly three hours from Hurghada.
